The book “Backup and Recovery” was published on February 6, 2007, almost twenty years ago. I was a technical reviewer for an earlier version of this book, “Unix Backup and Recovery”, published on January 1, 1999. And these books were not the first to advocate the standard 3-2-1 model of backups. Curtis also has more modern books, if you like — such as “Modern Data Protection: Ensuring Recoverability of All Modern Workloads”, published in 2021.

If you’re not adequately backing up your data, then that is entirely on you. After thirty-plus years of this best practice guidance, there is no excuse for that kind of incompetence.

Apple makes this pretty easy with iCloud and Time Machine, but they are far from the only company trying to make this as easy as possible for their customers.

While I was expressing an ideal setup, it isn’t all or nothing. A single backup is still better than none at all.

I suppose I didn’t specify exactly what I would recommend to someone who thinks it’s too hard, so here is that:

1. Install Backblaze. This is basically fire and forget. 2. (1) is enough for most people, but if interested (and on a Mac, which is what I’m familiar with), plug in an external SSD once a week or so for Time Machine. Setup involves clicking on the drive in the setup wizard and specifying an encryption password.

I don’t know about “ultra” robust, but this gives you protection from accidental deletions, natural disasters happening to your computer, hardware failures, and corruption from software bugs. The ongoing maintenance is plugging in a hard drive once a week.

If that is too much effort, just (1) provides natural disaster and hardware failure protection. It helps somewhat with the others but Backblaze only saves versions for 60 days and that’s a tight window to notice subtle corruption of e.g. your photos.

I agree, if it has too much friction it's more likely you will postpone it. Any option, either just a cloud backup tool or a spare HDD or SSD with CCC or TimeMachine is better than nothing. And you have to plan for the most likely case, e.g. spilling beer on the laptop vs the house burning down.

For the house burning scenario, a cheap strategy is having one or two old HDD's in USB cases, located somewhere away from your house, in a place you regularly visit and trust security-wise. For Apple devices, the storage is usually encrypted. And the encryption key is on the Secure Enclave, and cannot be exfiltrated.

So, if the machine dies, you can’t just take the SSD and solder it onto another board somewhere. Even if you could, the SSD is part of the SOC that includes the CPU, and the Secure Enclave is part of the logic board that it was soldered onto.

Recovering data from an Apple device is intentionally hard to do. Apple wants to protect that device as much as possible from anyone who might try to steal your data by simply unsoldering chips and soldering them back on somewhere else.

You're confusing different layers of encryption. The physical storage is indeed encrypted as bradknowles describes. Your iCloud-shareable keys ensure that only you can read your files. The hardware-level encryption ensures that an SSD can only be accessed from the SoC that it's paired with.

That’s a wipe and restore type option. Because the RAM and SSD are part of the SOC chip that also includes the CPU cores, the GPU cores, etc….

So, afterwards you effectively have a new iPhone with upgraded storage. Which you then have to restore somehow.

That is, unless you can find someone who can de-lid the SOC, remove the tiny RAM and/or SDD storage chips, and replace them with new ones. But then you’d have the same problem that the data was on the old chips, and encrypted. And so you can’t just copy that data over to the new chips, you have to decrypt all the data using the key stored on the Secure Enclave and copy it out in unencrypted format, then once the old chips are removed from the SOC and replaced, you then have to copy back all that data onto those new chips and have it re-encrypted from the Secure Enclave.

Anyone who can do that could just give you a new iPhone with more storage.

The actual key cannot be exfiltrated from the Secure Enclave. All the encryption/decryption is done inside the Secure Enclave. Knowing the owner’s password is just enough to let you pass data through the Secure Enclave to do the appropriate encryption/decryption operations.

So, you can’t copy that key over to a different Secure Enclave. If you could, then it would no longer be a Secure Enclave.

I mean the most frequent scenario is that the person trying to unlock the device is the one who owns it, yet we still have account passwords. You have to protect against the worst case. There is not a trusted enclave in existence (Apple, Intel, etc.) that will let you read its contents. That’s the point!

It's unrelated to the physical connection, but the drive encryption used on the built-in drive keeps its keys in the CPU's secure enclave, so dead CPU == data lost, regardless of whether the ssd itself is damaged.

Obviously if you used the same encryption scheme on a removable drive you'd hit the same issue - but most people don't do that, because storing the encryption keys in the Secure Enclave makes your drive effectively no longer removable.

The 5090 does have a bandwidth advantage, but also must pass more data from main to GPU memory for any particular task. Comparisons of a 5090 to a DGX Spark at 273 GB/s are illustrative since the Spark uses unified memory similar to Apple's M-series. [0] The 5090 certainly wins most benchmarks but that doesn't mean the DGX Spark is not useful.

0. https://float16.cloud/en-en/ai-benchmark/dgx-spark-vs-rtx-50...

Loading data to the GPU will generally never be the bottleneck. Yes that's a bit better for unified memory, but prefill and decode will still be bound by compute and memory bandwidth respectively.

There's some value in having a huge amount of memory addressable by the GPU for loading larger models, but even that doesn't make sense for current gen models. For MOE models, newer inference engines with smarter GPU expert caching and pinned memory allow a GPU with lots of bandwidth to significantly outperform a Spark, so that leaves you with larger dense models that fit on a spark but not on a GPU where you might have a use-case.

But even then it's hard. For instance a full-fat BF16 of a ~30B parameter model will fit on a 128GB spark and not a 32GB 5090, but at that size it's going to be frustratingly slow on the spark given the compute and bandwidth constraints.

Imo these devices are mostly good for experimentation, or if you only want to do overnight jobs or training which wouldn't be possible on a GPU, and you don't want to pay $100k for a DGX station.
